newsitem.title: GERMANY: Angry miners add threat of violence to Bonn woes.
newsitem.headline: Angry miners add threat of violence to Bonn woes.

text.p: Thousands of angry miners paralysing Bonn's government quarter in protest at planned subsidy cuts have added a new element to tension over Germany's austerity plans -- the threat of violence.

They seemed ready to take out their anger on Kohl himself as they broke through police barricades on Tuesday and rushed in the direction of the chancellery after Kohl called off a scheduled meeting with their union leaders.
"Kohl's a coward, he's got 10,000 people waiting and he won't come out," shouted miner Frank Koepper, 44.

Hundreds of burly protesters, many clad in overalls and hardhats, bounced aside a police van and smashed one of its windows before being stopped by riot police as they headed for the chancellery -- normally a demonstration-free zone.
The protesters, often with tattooed arms and coal-smudged faces, believed they had little to lose.
"No-one has any propects and we are very angry indeed. We don't think much of the principle of non-violent protest," said Frank Kocimr, 34, a miner from Duisburg.
Organisers said they were expecting up to 20,000 of Germany's 90,000 pitworkers to descend on the city, although it was not clear how many had actually come.

For a sleepy city used to demonstrations by smiling pacifists or disciplined office workers, the sight of tough working men blocking roads, clanking chains and littering the streets with beer cans and cigarette butts is threatening.
But for the men, the idea of quitting the industry their fathers and grandfathers worked in and which provided the basis of Germany's post-war economic miracle is no less menacing.
About 300 miners stripped down to their underwear and chanted, "Do you want the shirts off our backs?" as they waved their clothes in the air.

Already, they have seen their industry shrivel to a shadow of its former self. Of 173 mines working in 1957 as the post-war economic miracle boomed, less than 20 are operating now with 88,000 jobs. IG Bergbau fears the government plans will cut over half of those by 2005.

The miners have chained themselves to the doors at the headquarters of the liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP), their main target because of its plans for deep cuts in the state subsidies that keep Germany's expensive coal mines working.
When they heard Kohl had postponed the talks, miners pelted the FDP building with eggs, shouted "Cowardly pigs!" and vowed to stay until Kohl meets their union leaders on Thursday.

Small groups wandered around the blocked main street in front of the FDP building, waving black flags emblazoned with a skull and crossbones, blowing whistles and chanting the names of their mines as if at a football match.
Others strung up life-sized dummies in pit overalls by the neck in trees outside the FDP building. "Broken promises are murder," was written across the chest of one.
Swarms of black-helmeted bikers revving their rumbling engines added more machismo to a protest that at times seemed to teeter on the edge of chaos.

Many miners said they felt betrayed by their union. "The union isn't strong but the workers are. The unions have stayed quiet and cooperate more with the employers than the workers, we don't feel they represent us any more," said miner Kocimr.

But the gruff miners and the police officers watching them often chatted and joked together amiably. "Many policemen come from the mining region and they understand the frustration of these men," said police officer Thomas Sanders.
